openingProblem.problem: In 1945 the four Allies agreed to run Germany as a single unit and to make it democratic. By October 1949 there were two German states, one a parliamentary democracy and one a Soviet-backed dictatorship. Why did a democratic West German state emerge, and why only in the West?

chunks.title: Occupation and denazification, 1945–1946
chunks.body:
When Germany surrendered unconditionally in May 1945, the country was in ruins and its government had ceased to exist. Sovereignty passed to the four victorious powers, the USA, Britain, France and the USSR, which divided Germany into four zones. Berlin, deep inside the Soviet zone, was itself split into four sectors.

At **Potsdam** in July and August 1945 the Allies agreed on broad goals: "democratization", "denazification" and "decartelization". They agreed to treat the German economy as a single unit, but also allowed the Soviets to take goods and plant from their own zone and a share of reparations from the western zones. This contradiction made reparations divisive from the start.

**Denazification** showed how hard it was to rebuild democracy. On 8 May 1945 there were 8 million Nazis in Germany; in Bonn, 102 of 112 doctors had been Party members. Sixteen million questionnaires were completed in the western zones, and the Americans listed 3.5 million "chargeable cases". But the people with the skills to run the country were often former Nazis, and the questionnaires frequently served to whitewash them. In Bavaria about half the secondary teachers sacked by 1946 were back at work two years later. Konrad Adenauer, the future chancellor, publicly opposed denazification in May 1946, believing that confronting Germans with Nazi crimes would provoke a nationalist backlash. In 1949 the new Federal Republic ended all investigations into the past of civil servants and army officers.

This mattered because the Allies wanted a democratic Germany but needed experienced Germans to govern it, which meant that West German democracy was built with many people who had served the Nazi state.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Allies agreed on goals but not on methods.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Potsdam did agree on democratization and denazification.
Many cases never came before tribunals.
The Nazi party itself was abolished and banned.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Denazification failed to remove former Nazis from German public life.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Sixteen million questionnaires were completed, yet in Bavaria about half the secondary teachers sacked by 1946 were back two years later, and in 1949 the Federal Republic ended all investigations of civil servants.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the new democracy was staffed by many former Nazis, because their skills were needed to rebuild the country.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Adenauer argued that confronting Germans with their crimes would provoke a backlash, so leniency may have helped democracy take root.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Denazification therefore failed as a purge but may have succeeded in avoiding a nationalist reaction.

chunks.title: The road to division, 1946–1947
chunks.body:
Cooperation between the occupying powers broke down quickly. The western zones could not feed themselves: the British occupation cost $80 million a year against at most $29 million in reparations, and in May 1946 the American military governor, General Clay, stopped reparations deliveries from the US zone, accusing the Soviets of breaking the Potsdam agreement. Britain followed two months later.

In the Soviet zone, the Social Democrats were merged with the Communists in 1946, a move condemned by the SPD in the west. The communist leader Walter Ulbricht summed up the method: "it has to look democratic, but everything must be in our hands". When free elections were held in Berlin in October 1946, the Communists came far behind both the SPD and the Christian Democrats, and Soviet policy hardened.

Western policy shifted. In September 1946 the US Secretary of State, **James Byrnes**, told a German audience in Stuttgart that American forces would stay as long as an occupation was needed. At the end of 1946 the Americans and British fused the economies of their zones into the **Bizone**, whose federal structure became the prototype for the West German state. The decisive break came at the Moscow conference of foreign ministers in March–April 1947. Britain and the USA wanted to rebuild the western German economy; the Soviets wanted reparations from the west. In May 1947 the Bizone gained a German Economic Council, the first step towards a West German government.

Two party leaders shaped the new politics. **Konrad Adenauer** founded the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in 1945 to unite Catholics and Protestants in a Christian, democratic party. **Kurt Schumacher**, who had spent the Nazi years in concentration camps, rebuilt the Social Democrats (SPD) and demanded a united, neutral Germany, opposing Adenauer's turn to the West. The historian Mary Fulbrook calls division "an ad hoc unintended result of the emerging Cold War", not a planned outcome.

This mattered because the occupiers' disagreements over reparations and the economy hardened into rival systems, which meant that two German states became likely well before 1949.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Allies still formally sought German unity in early 1947.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Soviet methods alienated Germans in the west.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Communists had real support in some industrial areas.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Bizone was the prototype of West Germany.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It did not yet signify a firm division.

chunks.title: Currency reform and blockade, 1948–1949
chunks.body:
In 1948 the Western Allies moved decisively. On 1 June, meeting in London, they announced plans for a separate West German state. On 18 June a new currency, the **Deutsche Mark**, was announced, and three days later it went into circulation. Ludwig Erhard, director of the Bizone's Economic Council, oversaw its introduction. The reform was unpopular at first, because it destroyed savings and pushed up prices, but it was quickly accepted as shops filled with goods that farmers and traders were now willing to sell.

Stalin's answer was the **Berlin blockade**. On 23 June the Soviets cut the rail links to the city. The Western powers responded with an airlift, which from 26 June 1948 to 12 May 1949 delivered about 2.3 million tons of supplies on 277,500 flights, at the cost of 73 Allied airmen. Stalin wanted to force the West either to leave Berlin or to abandon a West German state. He achieved neither.

Instead, the blockade made the Western powers more determined, and it made division more acceptable to Germans themselves. In April 1949 France joined the Bizone, creating a western economic unit of 49 million people against 17 million in the Soviet zone. Judt concludes that the Berlin crisis led directly to the creation of two German states, an outcome none of the Allies had sought four years earlier.

This mattered because the currency reform created a western economy and the blockade turned Western Germans and the Allies into partners, which meant that a separate West German state became both possible and popular.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The currency reform created a separate western economy.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Few Allies had wanted division in 1945.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the significance of the currency reform for the emergence of the Federal Republic between 1948 and 1949.
To what extent was the Cold War the main reason for the emergence of a separate West German state between 1945 and 1949?

useItInAnEssay.claim: The currency reform was the decisive economic step towards a West German state.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Announced on 18 June 1948 and overseen by Erhard, the Deutsche Mark was quickly accepted as shops filled with goods.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the western zones now had their own economy, so Stalin answered with the Berlin blockade.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, it was the blockade that made division politically acceptable, as Judt argues, and France joined the Bizone only in April 1949.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The currency reform was therefore significant because it made division economic before it became political.

chunks.title: The Basic Law and the birth of the Federal Republic, 1948–1949
chunks.body:
In 1948 a **Parliamentary Council** met in Bonn, under Adenauer's presidency and close Allied supervision, to draft a constitution for the western zones. Bottaro and Stanley describe the **Basic Law** (Grundgesetz) as a provisional constitution for the western zones; until 1990 it applied only to West Germany. Its authors set out to avoid the weaknesses that had destroyed the Weimar Republic.

The president was to be largely ceremonial, elected by parliament for five years and re-electable only once, without the emergency powers of Weimar's Article 48. The Bundestag could remove a chancellor only through a **constructive vote of no confidence**, which required a majority for a named successor. Half the Bundestag was elected in constituencies and half by proportional representation from party lists, and parties that worked against the constitution could be banned. There were to be no referenda or plebiscites, which the Nazis had exploited. Power was divided with the federal states (Länder).

The Parliamentary Council approved the Basic Law on 8 May 1949, and it came into force later that month. In the first Bundestag election on **14 August 1949** the CDU/CSU won 139 seats, the SPD 131 and the Free Democrats 52. On 15 September Adenauer was elected chancellor by a majority of one vote, heading a coalition with the FDP, whose leader Theodor Heuss became president. Stalin responded by creating the **German Democratic Republic** on 7 October 1949. West Germany was not yet sovereign: Allied High Commissioners replaced military government and kept powers to intervene.

This mattered because the Basic Law combined strong, stable government with protections against extremism, which meant that West Germany's second attempt at democracy began with lessons learned from the first.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Basic Law corrected Weimar's weaknesses.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was drafted under Allied influence.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The 1949 election gave democracy a narrow start.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Adenauer won by a single vote.
West Germany was not yet sovereign.

howItGetsAsked: Analyse the ways in which the Basic Law of 1949 sought to avoid the weaknesses of the Weimar constitution.
Evaluate the significance of the currency reform for the emergence of the Federal Republic between 1948 and 1949.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Basic Law strengthened government against the instability that had destroyed Weimar.
useItInAnEssay.prove: It introduced the constructive vote of no confidence and replaced pure PR with a mixed system, while the president lost Weimar's Article 48 emergency powers.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a chancellor could not be removed without a majority for a successor, so governments lasted longer.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the Basic Law was drafted under Allied supervision, and Adenauer was elected in 1949 by only one vote.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The Basic Law therefore created the structures for stability, even before stability itself had been achieved.

This meant that former Nazis staffed the new state, because their skills were needed to rebuild it.
However, Adenauer argued that confronting Germans with their crimes would provoke a nationalist backlash, and the new democracy survived.
The claim is therefore valid for denazification as a purge, but not for its effect on the survival of democracy.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the significance of the currency reform for the emergence of the Federal Republic between 1948 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The significance of the currency reform
decodeKey.scope: The emergence of the Federal Republic
decodeKey.judgement: Decisive step, or one among several?

modelPlan.thesis: The currency reform was highly significant, because it created a separate western economy and provoked the blockade that made division acceptable; but the political decision for a West German state had already been taken in London in June 1948.

arguments.claim: Limits: the London decision and the Basic Law.

modelPlan.counter: The Allies had announced plans for a West German state on 1 June 1948, before the currency reform.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Was it decisive? It made division economic and provoked the crisis that made it political.

segments.text: The currency reform was the decisive economic step towards the Federal Republic.
Announced on 18 June 1948 and overseen by Erhard, the Deutsche Mark was quickly accepted as shops filled with goods.
This meant that the western zones had their own economy, so Stalin answered with the blockade, which made division acceptable to Germans.
However, the Western Allies had already announced plans for a separate state on 1 June 1948, and the Basic Law came only in 1949.
The currency reform was therefore significant as the point at which division became practical as well as planned.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons for, and the results of, the creation of the Bizone between 1946 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which result was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The Bizone was created because the occupation was too costly and the reparations dispute had broken four-power cooperation; its main result was a federal prototype for the West German state.

arguments.claim: Reason: the cost of the occupation.
Result: the Economic Council and the currency reform.

modelPlan.counter: Judt notes the Bizone did not yet signify a firm division.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result mattered most? The federal prototype for the Federal Republic.

segments.text: The Bizone was created because the western occupiers could not afford to run their zones separately.
The British occupation cost far more than it earned in reparations, and Clay stopped reparations to the Soviets in May 1946.
This meant that fusing the economies was the only practical way to feed Germans, so the zones were combined at the end of 1946.
However, Judt notes that the Bizone did not yet signify a firm division; that came after the Moscow conference of 1947.
The most significant result was therefore the federal structure that became the prototype for the West German state.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the ways in which the Basic Law of 1949 sought to avoid the weaknesses of the Weimar constitution.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Ways the Basic Law avoided Weimar's weaknesses
decodeKey.judgement: Which change mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The Basic Law avoided Weimar's weaknesses by strengthening the chancellor, weakening the president, reducing pure proportional representation and allowing anti-democratic parties to be banned.

arguments.claim: The constructive vote of no confidence.

modelPlan.counter: The Basic Law was drafted under Allied supervision, which suggests its design was not entirely German.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which change mattered most? The constructive vote of no confidence, which secured stable government.

segments.text: The Basic Law's most important change was to make governments harder to bring down.
Under the constructive vote of no confidence, the Bundestag could remove a chancellor only by electing a successor, and the president lost Weimar's Article 48 emergency powers.
This meant that the serial instability of Weimar could not recur, so strong chancellors such as Adenauer could govern for long periods.
However, the Basic Law was drafted under close Allied supervision, and it was a provisional constitution for the western zones only.
The Basic Law therefore corrected Weimar's main weakness, unstable government, while guarding against extremism.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the role of Konrad Adenauer in the emergence of a democratic West German state between 1945 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: How far did the outcome depend on him?

modelPlan.thesis: Adenauer played a central role by founding the CDU, presiding over the Parliamentary Council and winning the first chancellorship; but the framework was set by the Allies and the Cold War.

arguments.claim: Limits: Allied control and the one-vote majority.

modelPlan.counter: The Allies supervised the drafting of the Basic Law and kept powers of intervention.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How far did it depend on him? On the shape of the new state, much; on its existence, little.

segments.text: Adenauer shaped the new democracy, but did not create the conditions for it.
He founded the CDU in 1945 to unite Catholics and Protestants, presided over the Parliamentary Council from 1948, and became chancellor in September 1949.
This meant that West Germany began with a broad centre-right party committed to democracy and the West.
However, the Allies supervised the Basic Law and kept powers of intervention, and Adenauer won the chancellorship by only one vote.
Adenauer's role was therefore decisive for the character of the new state, while the Cold War decided its existence.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the political development of the western zones and the Soviet zone of Germany between 1945 and 1949.
essayQuestions.scope: the western zones and the Soviet zone of Germany

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout
decodeKey.scope: The western zones and the Soviet zone
decodeKey.judgement: How and why did the two parts diverge?

modelPlan.thesis: Both parts of Germany began under four-power occupation with the shared aims agreed at Potsdam, but the western zones developed competing parties, free elections and a democratic Basic Law, whereas in the Soviet zone the SPD was merged with the Communists and power was kept in Communist hands, producing two states in 1949.

arguments.claim: Similarity: a common starting point at Potsdam.
Difference: elections and the Basic Law.

modelPlan.counter: Both parts were governed under occupation, and the western Basic Law itself was drafted under close Allied monitoring.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Why did they diverge? Because the occupiers' aims diverged, as Fulbrook's 'unintended result of the emerging Cold War' suggests.

segments.text: The western zones and the Soviet zone began together but developed opposite political systems.

In the Soviet zone the SPD was amalgamated with the Communists in 1946, and Ulbricht insisted 'it has to look democratic, but everything must be in our hands', whereas in the west the CDU, SPD and FDP competed in the free election of 14 August 1949.
This meant that the west developed genuine party competition, so the Basic Law could found a parliamentary democracy, while the east was controlled by one party.
However, both parts were shaped by their occupiers, and the western Basic Law was itself drafted under close Allied monitoring.
The two parts therefore diverged because their occupiers did, producing a democratic Federal Republic and a Communist GDR in 1949.
